## The idea

Play the white notes from C to the next C and you hear a shape that has supplied
melodies for centuries. Start the same white-note walk on D and the shape
changes, although the keys under your fingers look similar. The useful object is
the spacing between notes. A *major scale* is the ordered step formula
`2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1`, measured in semitones.

I used to treat scales as tables of note names. That makes twelve major scales
look like twelve facts. The formula turns them into one function and twelve
inputs. It also makes the two small gaps audible. Those one-semitone steps sit
between degrees 3 and 4, then 7 and 8. Move either gap and the scale loses its
major shape.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 112
use_synth :pluck

define :build_scale do |root, steps|
  notes = [root]
  steps.each { |step| notes << notes[-1] + step }
  notes
end

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.32
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

major_steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1]
c_major = build_scale(note(:c4), major_steps)

play_phrase c_major
play_phrase c_major.reverse

thirds = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 7]
play_phrase thirds.map { |index| c_major[index] }

(60...72).each do |root|
  ours = build_scale(root, major_steps)
  sonic_pi = scale(root, :major).to_a
  puts "root #{root}: #{ours == sonic_pi}"
end
```

The first pass climbs and descends in adjacent steps. The last pass keeps
leaping over one scale degree, so the same collection sounds less like an
exercise and more like a line with direction. The log prints `true` for each
root when the constructor agrees with Sonic Pi's built-in scale.

## Change one thing

1. Change the root from `:c4` to `:fs3`. The interval pattern survives the new
   starting point. Listen for the same large-step, small-step contour at a lower
   register.
2. Change the fourth value in `major_steps` from `2` to `1`. The final note now
   lands a semitone short of the octave. The error accumulates because the
   formula describes distances, not destinations.
3. Play `c_major.values_at(0, 2, 4, 7)` slowly. You hear three stacked skips and
   then the octave. Remove index `7` and hear how the remaining notes imply a
   chord rather than a completed scale.

## Why it works

Each entry in the formula is a delta. `build_scale` performs a cumulative sum,
keeping every intermediate value. Programmers meet the same operation in path
lengths, account balances, and time-series data. The root supplies the initial
state; the step array supplies transitions.

The sum is twelve, so the final value is one octave above the root. Five entries
are whole tones of two semitones and two are semitones. Their order creates the
major scale. Rotation preserves the values while moving the small gaps, which
will produce the modes in Lesson 24. Changing the root is transposition because
every output receives the same offset.

The comparison loop is a useful kind of musical test. It checks the algorithm
against Sonic Pi across all twelve pitch classes rather than trusting one C
example. Ruby equality compares the arrays element by element. Syntax checking
cannot tell us whether the notes sound right, so the listening pass remains
part of the work.

## Take it further

Write `descending_scale(root, steps)` without calling `reverse`. It must begin
at `root + 12`, subtract the step values in reverse order, and finish exactly on
`root`. Print the ascending and descending arrays for all twelve roots, then
play the pair in F major. The structural constraint is that both arrays contain
eight notes and meet at the same octave.
